clinical_knowledge.topic: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Admit for stroke unit monitoring (high early stroke risk post-TIA), dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300mg + clopidogrel 75mg), statin, BP control, carotid imaging, ECG monitoring x72h for paroxysmal AF, patient education on FAST warning signs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Focal seizure without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any recurrence of symptoms — signals ongoing high stroke risk.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 67F with HTN, hypercholesterolaemia, T2DM presents with sudden-onset right arm weakness and dysarthria lasting ~20 min then completely resolving. First episode. No headache or visual loss.
reference_soap.objective: Neurological exam (currently normal), BP both arms, ECG (AF?), bloods: FBC, glucose, lipids, coag, CT head (rule out haemorrhage), carotid Doppler, echo if indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: TIA — high stroke risk. ABCD2 score required. DDx: focal seizure, hypoglycaemia, hemiplegic migraine, Todd's paresis.
reference_soap.plan: Admit for stroke unit monitoring (high early stroke risk post-TIA), dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300mg + clopidogrel 75mg), statin, BP control, carotid imaging, ECG monitoring x72h for paroxysmal AF, patient education on FAST warning signs.

learning_objectives: Characterise TIA: sudden onset, brief duration, complete resolution
Calculate ABCD2 score and explain stroke urgency
Counsel patient who is reluctant to stay in hospital

teaching.one_liner: A brief episode of stroke-like symptoms that fully resolves within minutes to hours — the danger isn't the episode itself but the high risk of a real stroke in the days that follow, so it's treated as a medical emergency, not a relief.
red_flags: Any recurrence of symptoms — signals ongoing high stroke risk

must_ask.say: What exactly happened, and how long did it last before it went away completely?

history.answer: My right arm suddenly went weak and my speech became slurred this morning, but it completely cleared up after about twenty minutes.
My right arm felt heavy and clumsy so I couldn't hold anything, but I didn't feel any numbness or pins and needles.
It was just my right arm and my speech; my legs felt completely normal and my left side was fine.
It started suddenly around eight o'clock this morning while I was eating breakfast, and I was completely normal right before that.
The arm weakness and slurred speech lasted about twenty minutes, and then everything went completely back to normal.
No, this was the very first time anything like this has ever happened to me.
I dropped my spoon and couldn't lift my teacup, but I was able to walk without stumbling.
Nothing brought it on, and moving my neck, arms, or changing position didn't make any difference.
No, I don't have any neck pain, back pain, or pain shooting down my arms.
My tongue felt thick and my words sounded slurred to my daughter, but my face didn't droop and I had no trouble swallowing.
No, my vision was completely normal with no blurriness, double vision, or dark spots.
No, I didn't have any headache before, during, or after it happened.
No, I stayed completely awake and aware the entire time, without passing out or any shaking.
No, I haven't had any chest pain, tightness, or racing heart sensations.
No, my bowel and bladder habits have been completely normal, with no accidents or numbness down below.
No shortness of breath, no difficulty chewing or swallowing, and my eyelids never drooped.
No, I haven't noticed any muscle twitching, jumping, or shrinking in my arms or legs.
No, I haven't had any cold, fever, chills, or diarrhea in the past few weeks.
I have had high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and type two diabetes for years, but I've never had an irregular heartbeat.
My blood sugar stays around one hundred to one hundred twenty on my pills, I eat a regular diet with meat, and I've never had stomach surgery.
No, I've never taken steroids, water pills, or cancer medications.
No, I don't do repetitive wrist work, lean on my elbows, or sit cross-legged for long periods.
I honestly thought I was just overtired and stressed from taking care of the house.
My daughter got very scared when she heard my speech and insisted on bringing me in, even though I told her it wasn't serious.
Since I feel completely back to normal now, I'm hoping I can just go home soon to look after my grandchildren.
I have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and type two diabetes, all diagnosed about ten years ago.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty-five, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take amlodipine five milligrams in the morning, atorvastatin forty milligrams at bedtime, and metformin five hundred milligrams twice daily.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I'm a retired schoolteacher living with my husband, and I am completely independent in my daily life.
My father had a stroke in his seventies, and my mother had high blood pressure.
